The stone beneath is cool through the fabric, old enough that the heat of Yavin's jungle never quite reaches it. Master Skywalker passes behind you — you hear the soft drag of his robe hem on stone, feel the ripple of his presence in the Force like a current you can almost ride if you stop trying. Below your knees, through the layers of temple floor — jungle-heated surface, then cool interior stone, then the dead air of spaces no one has entered in years — you reach for what you felt that morning: the pressure, the weight, the thing in the dark. turns.narration_excerpt: You ask him to carry it. So he does. Luke settles onto the cushion beside yours, folding his legs with the practiced ease of a man who has meditated in worse places—ice caves, asteroid tunnels, the back of a landspeeder. He looks at the stone floor, not at you. "There are levels beneath this one," he says. "Twelve layers of Massassi construction, then the original Sith foundations. The ones who came before the Massassi—they built into the rock itself." He pauses. "What you felt was a vergence. A
choices: Wait. You want to understand more before you say anything. Ask him what he's learned from the archives—what the old Order wrote about the vergence. Knowledge first, position second.

Push. "Then study it. The old Order sealed things—you said it yourself. What they sealed festered. If you leave this untouched, someone else will find it later, with less warning than I just had." Let him hear your conviction.
Ask a different question entirely. "Kira's cushion was empty this morning. She's been gone before. Do you know where she goes?" The vergence can wait. The friend can't.
Let him walk away. Sit here, in the cool stone, and feel what the vergence feels like when you're not reaching for it. Passivity is also a choice.

The silence stretches long enough that you hear your own breathing, the distant drip of condensation from a stone lintel somewhere below. "I know she leaves," he says. "I don't know where."
